OUTSIDE THE BIBLE · NINTH CENTURY BC; FOUND AT DIBON ON 19 AUGUST 1868
Mesha Stele: Omri and his son
Dibon and the places of the account
The nations. Only places Scripture names are shown, each where the Atlas puts it.
“Mesha king of Moab was a sheepmaster, and rendered unto the king of Israel an hundred thousand lambs, and an hundred thousand rams, with the wool.” 2 Kings 3:4
“When Ahab was dead … the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel.” 2 Kings 3:5 2 Kings 1:1
Besieged, “he took with him seven hundred men that drew swords, to break through even unto the king of Edom: but they could not”. 2 Kings 3:26

“Then he took his eldest son that should have reigned in his stead, and offered him for a burnt offering upon the wall. And there was great indignation against Israel: and they departed from him, and returned to their own land.” 2 Kings 3:27
He offered his eldest son as a burnt offering upon the wall of his besieged city. 2 Kings 3:27
Outside the BibleOn his stele he gives the glory to his god: “I made this high place for Chemosh”, and “Chemosh drave him out from before me”.[12]

Outside the BibleThe stele lists his building: Baal-meon, Qiryathen, Aroer and “the highway by the Arnon”, Beth-Bamoth, Bezer, Medeba and Beth-Diblathen; and he says he cut “the cutting for QRHH” (a place named on the stele) “with the help of prisoner[s of] Israel”.[12]
Tribute to the king of Israel in wool and flocks, until his revolt. 2 Kings 3:4–5
Against him stood Israel, Judah and Edom together. 2 Kings 3:9
“They gathered all that were able to put on armour, and upward, and stood in the border.” 2 Kings 3:21
The allies were told to “mar every good piece of land with stones”, and did so. 2 Kings 3:19 2 Kings 3:25
The prophets who spoke about him
El Elisha “he will deliver the Moabites also into your hand”
PLACED BY ISRAEL'S KINGS (THIELE, AS REVISED BY MCFALL AND YOUNG)

No year of his own is known. Kings dates his revolt after Ahab's death (853 BC on the main system) and the war against him to the reign of Jehoram of Israel (852–841 BC). Driver (1890) calls his inscription a monument of the ninth century BC.
2 Kings 1:1 and 3:5; A. H. Sayce, ISBE (1915), p. 2072
Sayce takes the stele's “forty” as “an indefinite period of time” and writes that “the revolt of Mesha took place after Ahab's death”. 2 Kings 1:1 [13]
In the middle of Ahab's reign
S. R. Driver (1890), pp. lxxxviii–lxxxix and xciv
Driver reads the stele's “half his son’s days” as Ahab's and concludes that the revolt took place “in the middle of Ahab's reign, not after his death (as stated, 2 Ki. 1, 1)”.[12]
A real discrepancy in the forty years

Ewing counts only 34 years for Omri and Ahab together, 23 if half of Ahab's reign is taken, and writes: “So great a difference cannot be explained by the use of round numbers.” 1 Kings 16:23 1 Kings 16:29 [14]
Scripture does not name Mesha's father, his capital or his god; Chemosh, Dibon and his father's name come from the stele.
Scripture gives no length of reign and does not tell what became of Mesha after Israel withdrew.
Isaiah 15–16 and Jeremiah 48, the oracles on Moab, do not name him.
The stele says nothing of the campaign of 2 Kings 3, and 2 Kings says nothing of the stele's wars at Ataroth, Nebo and Yahaz.

From the textMesha king of Moab (2 Kings 3:4); not Caleb's son Mesha (1 Chronicles 2:42) or the Benjamite Mesha (1 Chronicles 8:9). Kings names him once; the rest of the chapter calls him “the king of Moab”. 2 Kings 3:4 2 Kings 3:26

Scholars' viewThe Mesha of the stele, “son of Chemoshmelek, king of Moab, the Daibonite”, is taken to be this king: Driver writes that the inscription “gives particulars of the revolt of Moab from Israel, noticed briefly in 2 Ki. 1, 1 = 3, 5”.[12]
